title: American Airlines 1
summary: American Airlines Flight 1 rolled over and crashed into Jamaica Bay two minutes after taking off from Idlewild Airport on 1 March 1962, killing all 87 passengers and eight crew aboard. During a left turn to 290 degrees at 1,600 ft, the Boeing 707 banked too sharply, rolled past 90 degrees, and entered a nearly vertical, upside-down dive before striking Pumpkin Patch Channel. The CAB traced the cause to a short circuit in wires damaged during manufacturing at a Bendix plant, producing a rudder malfunction that led to a loss of control from which the crew could not recover.
probable_cause: Rudder control system malfunction producing yaw, sideslip, and roll leading to a loss of control from which recovery was not effective; a rudder servo malfunction due to shorted wires was cited as the most likely abnormality.

factors.evidence: CAB inspectors ... discovered workers using tweezers to bind up bundles of wires, thereby damaging them
a short circuit caused by wires in the automatic piloting system that had been damaged in the manufacturing process
rudder control system malfunction producing yaw, sideslip, and roll
the aircraft banked too sharply, rolled past 90°, and began an upside-down, nose-first descent in a nearly vertical dive

events.text: The aircraft received instructions to taxi to Runway 31L at 09:54 EST.
At 10:02 the crew received clearance to proceed to Los Angeles nonstop under instrument flight rules.
The aircraft became airborne at 10:07 and, following departure control instructions, initiated a left turn to a heading of 290 degrees.
In the course of the turn, at 1,600 ft, the aircraft banked too sharply, rolled past 90 degrees, and began an upside-down, nose-first descent in a nearly vertical dive.
The Boeing 707 crashed into Pumpkin Patch Channel, Jamaica Bay, at 10:08:49 while angled at 78 degrees, exploding on impact.

title: Flying Tiger Line 739
summary: Flying Tiger Line Flight 739, a Lockheed Super Constellation chartered by the US Army, disappeared on 16 March 1962 while en route from Guam to the Philippines with 107 military personnel and crew aboard. A civilian tanker observed what appeared to be an in-flight explosion. The Civil Aeronautics Board determined Flight 739 probably exploded in-flight based on tanker observations.
probable_cause: Based on observations by a civilian tanker of an apparent in-flight explosion, the Civil Aeronautics Board determined Flight 739 probably exploded in-flight, though an exact cause could not be determined without examining aircraft remnants.

factors.evidence: A civilian tanker observed what appeared to be an in-flight explosion believed to be the missing Super Constellation
The aircraft was not seen or heard from again after the final position report
one of the largest air and sea searches in the history of the Pacific was conducted though no trace of wreckage or debris was ever recovered
This was the deadliest single-aircraft aviation accident involving the Super Constellation

events.text: The aircraft departed from Guam at 12:57 GMT with an estimated time of arrival at the Philippines at 19:16 GMT.
Eighty minutes after departure, at 14:22 GMT, the captain radioed a routine message and gave his position as being 280 nautical miles west of Guam.
At 15:39 the Guam radio operator attempted to contact Flight 739 for a position report but was unable to establish contact.
A civilian tanker observed what appeared to be an in-flight explosion believed to be the missing Super Constellation.
The aircraft was not seen or heard from again.
Despite an extensive search, no trace of wreckage or debris was ever recovered.

notes: No wreckage or debris recovered, exact cause could not be determined

title: Air France 007
summary: Air France Flight 007, a Boeing 707 taking off from Orly on 3 June 1962, lifted off but the main landing gear remained on the ground. The crew attempted to abort the takeoff, using wheel brakes and reverse thrust to stop the aircraft. The aircraft skidded off the runway and struck the town of Villeneuve-le-Roi. Investigation indicated the elevator trim motor may have failed.
probable_cause: A motor driving the elevator trim may have failed, leaving the crew unable to complete rotation and takeoff.

title: Alitalia 771
summary: Alitalia Flight 771, a multi-leg service from Sydney to Rome, crashed into a hill about 84 km north-east of Bombay on approach on 7-8 July 1962, killing all 94 aboard. Investigators found navigational errors led the captain, on his first familiarization trip over the Bangkok-Bombay leg, to believe he was closer to his destination than he actually was, causing a premature descent for a straight-in instrument approach at night; the aircraft continued down to 3,600 ft, below both the 9,000 ft minimum safety altitude and the 4,000 ft minimum initial approach altitude, before striking terrain.
probable_cause: Errors in navigation led the pilot to think he was closer to the point of descent than in reality, resulting in a premature descent for a straight-in instrument approach at night and controlled flight into terrain.

factors.evidence: Unfamiliarity of the pilot with the terrain on the route
a premature descent for a straight-in instrument approach at night
errors in navigation which led the pilot to believe that he was nearer to his destination than he actually was

resulting in ... controlled flight into terrain

events.text: Flight 771 departed Bangkok at 15:16 UTC with 94 people aboard according to the load sheet, though the flight plan stated 98, and the plan had not been signed by the pilot-in-command.
At 17:20 the flight first contacted Bombay Flight Information Center, requesting a weather forecast and stating its ETA as 18:45 at an altitude of 36,000 ft.
At 18:20 the flight switched to the Bombay approach frequency and was approved to descend over Aurangabad to 20,000 ft.
By 18:38:54 the DC-8 had reached 5,000 ft and continued descending to 3,600 ft, well below the 9,000 ft minimum safety altitude and the 4,000 ft minimum initial approach altitude.
The aircraft crashed into a hill about 84 km north-east of Bombay while on approach, killing all 94 aboard.

notes: No national investigating agency is named in the text; ICAO is cited as the source of the secondary causes list.

title: Varig 810

route.from_name: Rio de Janeiro/Galeão – Antonio Carlos Jobim International Airport

summary: Varig Flight 810 crashed into the Laz Cruz Peak while maneuvering for an approach to Lima on 27 November 1962, killing all 97 aboard. An overestimate of seven minutes in the flight-planned time between Pisco and Lima left the Boeing 707 too high for a straight-in approach to runway 33, so ATC had the crew fly a 360-degree orbit and turns to intercept the ILS back course; during this extended maneuvering the aircraft deviated eight miles east of the published approach track and struck the peak at a heading of 333 degrees. Investigators suggested the pilot may have mistuned the Limatambo NDB for the Lima NDB.
probable_cause: A deviation, for reasons unknown, from the track prescribed for the instrument approach along the ILS back course of Lima-Callao Airport.

factors.evidence: the flight was still too high for a straight-in approach to runway 33, ATC suggested that the aircraft make a 360° orbit over Las Palmas
the aircraft crashed into the Laz Cruz Peak, eight miles east of the approach track for the published ILS procedure
it was possible that the pilot incorrectly tuned to the Limatambo non-directional beacon in the belief it was the 335-KHz Lima NDB
the aircraft struck the peak eight miles east of the approach track for the published ILS procedure

events.text: At 03:43 UTC the flight departed Rio en route to Lima carrying 80 passengers and 17 crew members.
The crew established contact with Lima air traffic control at 08:09 while at 36,000 ft, giving an estimate of overflying Pisco at 08:13.
At 08:30, with the flight at 12,000 ft directly overhead Las Palmas and still too high for a straight-in approach to runway 33, ATC had the crew fly a 360-degree orbit over Las Palmas.
The flight continued turning to intercept the ILS back course at a heading of 327 degrees before initiating a turn north.
At a heading of 333 degrees the aircraft crashed into the Laz Cruz Peak, eight miles east of the approach track for the published ILS procedure.
Communications with air traffic control ceased at 08:37, and an emergency was declared at 08:55.

notes: Official probable cause cites an unexplained deviation from the approach track; the mistuned-NDB and equipment-malfunction theories are noted in the text as unconfirmed possibilities.
No investigating agency named in the text.
